answer:
Combine models asynchronous work as a typed pipeline built from four roles.

- **Publisher** — emits a stream of values and one completion (finished or failure). Carries Output and Failure associated types.
- **Subscriber** — receives values, completion and demand signals. You rarely write one by hand; `sink` and `assign` cover almost everything.
- **Operator** — a method on Publisher returning a new publisher (map, filter, flatMap, debounce). Lazy: nothing flows until someone subscribes.
- **Subscription** — the link between publisher and subscriber, torn down through `AnyCancellable`.

Positioning matters in a 2026 interview. Combine shipped with iOS 13 and Apple has added essentially nothing to it since, steering new code to async/await, AsyncSequence and the Observation framework. It is still the right tool inside an existing Combine code base, for `ObservableObject`/`@Published` plumbing, and where you need declarative multi-stream composition (debounce plus combineLatest) with cancellation for free.

Subjects are publishers you can imperatively send values into — the bridge between non-Combine code and a Combine pipeline.

- **PassthroughSubject\<Output, Failure>** — broadcasts values to current subscribers as they arrive. It holds no value, so a subscriber that arrives late sees nothing that happened before.
- **CurrentValueSubject\<Output, Failure>** — holds a current value, set in the initializer and readable through `.value`. A new subscriber gets that value immediately, then every later update.

Use PassthroughSubject for events (button taps, gestures) and CurrentValueSubject for state (a loading flag, the current user).

In new code the equivalents usually live outside Combine: `@Observable` for view state, and `AsyncStream` with its continuation for wrapping a delegate or callback API. Reach for a Subject when the surrounding pipeline is already Combine, or when you need to hand callers an `AnyPublisher` because that is what the existing API vends.

Combine operators group into five jobs: transform, filter, combine, rate-limit and schedule.

- map / tryMap / compactMap — transform values; tryMap can throw.
- **filter / removeDuplicates** — drop values you do not want.
- **flatMap** — chain into another publisher; the tool for dependent requests.
- combineLatest / merge / zip — join several streams.
- **debounce / throttle** — control firing rate (typeahead, scroll).
- retry / catch / replaceError — error handling.
- receive(on:) / subscribe(on:) — choose the scheduler for downstream and upstream work respectively.
- assign(to:on:) / assign(to:) — bind output to a property without writing a `sink`.
- **share / multicast** — share one subscription's work across several subscribers.
- eraseToAnyPublisher() — type-erase at API boundaries.

Be deliberate about scheduling: by default work runs on whichever queue the publisher chose, so UI updates need `.receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)`.

Currency note worth saying out loud: Swift Async Algorithms now offers the same combinators — debounce, throttle, combineLatest, merge, zip, removeDuplicates — over AsyncSequence, so a greenfield target can get this composition without Combine at all.

SwiftUI observes a Combine-based view model through `ObservableObject` and `@Published`.

- **ObservableObject** — a reference type with a built-in `objectWillChange` publisher.
- **@Published** — a property wrapper that routes every mutation into `objectWillChange`, so views observing the object re-render.
- @StateObject when the view owns the object, @ObservedObject when someone else owns it, @EnvironmentObject for shared state injected down the tree.
- Custom pipelines feeding the UI must keep their cancellables alive in a `Set<AnyCancellable>`.

The caveat that makes this a modern question: `objectWillChange` invalidates the WHOLE view, so a change to any property re-renders every observer. The Observation framework (`@Observable`, held in a plain `@State`, iOS 17 and later) tracks individual property reads instead and is the default for new SwiftUI code — an `@Observable` class needs no Combine at all.

Keep Combine here for the stream work SwiftUI has no answer for: debounced typeahead, combineLatest over several sources, retrying network composition.

Combine and async/await interoperate in both directions, and Apple's direction of travel points from Combine toward async/await.

- **Publisher → async** — `.values` exposes an AsyncSequence; iterate it with `for await`.
- **async → Publisher** — wrap the call in a `Future`, or push results into a Subject from a `Task`.
- `assign(to: &$prop)` binds a publisher straight into a `@Published` property.
- `Task { @MainActor in ... }` inside a sink is the bridge into actor-isolated mutation.

Under Swift 6 strict concurrency the seams show: Combine predates Sendable and has no isolation model, so sink closures that hop isolation domains produce warnings or errors. The fix is normally to end the pipeline early and continue the work inside a Task.

Guideline: write new code with async/await, AsyncStream and Swift Async Algorithms. Reach for Combine when you are already inside a Combine code base, when you need `ObservableObject`/`@Published` interop, or when a UIKit-era API only vends a publisher.

Most Combine bugs come from a pipeline that was never retained, retained too strongly, or delivered on the wrong scheduler.

- **Discarding the AnyCancellable** — the subscription is torn down immediately and nothing ever fires. Always `.store(in: &bag)`.
- Strong capture of self in `sink` — a retain cycle; use `[weak self]`.
- **Wrong scheduler for UI** — UI mutation must land on `DispatchQueue.main` (or `RunLoop.main`) via `.receive(on:)`.
- **Re-running expensive upstream work** — without `.share()` or `.multicast()` every new subscriber replays the whole chain.
- Tearing down on the first error — most operators complete on failure; use `.catch` / `.replaceError` when the stream must survive.
- `.assign(to:on:)` retains its target — prefer `.assign(to: &$prop)`, which binds to a `@Published` without retaining.
- **Unbounded demand** — Combine is demand-driven, but `sink` requests unlimited. With a high-rate source add `.collect`, `.throttle`, or a custom subscriber.
- Sendable friction under Swift 6 — hop out of the pipeline with `Task { @MainActor in ... }` rather than mutating actor-isolated state inside a sink.

Switching to the latest inner publisher is the fix, because `flatMap` keeps every request alive and merges their results, so a slow early response can land after a fast late one.

- `flatMap` subscribes to each inner publisher and merges the outputs, running them all at once unless you cap it. That is the right behaviour for independent work such as uploading five images.
- `map` into a publisher followed by `switchToLatest` cancels the previous inner subscription every time a new value arrives, which is cancel-previous semantics and exactly what a typeahead needs.
- `flatMap(maxPublishers: .max(1))` serialises instead: the next inner publisher starts only when the previous one finishes, which suits a queue where order matters.
- Put `debounce` and `removeDuplicates` in front so you are not issuing a request per character, and `receive(on:)` at the end before touching the UI.
- The typing catches people out: the inner publisher's `Failure` has to match the outer one's, so in practice you `catch` inside the inner publisher and emit a value-shaped result rather than letting one failure end the whole stream.
- In async/await the same pattern is a stored `Task` you cancel before starting the next one, which is fewer moving parts if the surrounding code is already async.

Three, because every subscription runs the whole chain again unless you deliberately multicast the publisher.

- A Combine publisher is a recipe rather than a running stream. Subscribing is what starts the work, and each subscriber gets its own subscription and its own upstream execution.
- `share()` wraps the upstream in a multicast over a `PassthroughSubject` with `autoconnect`, so subscribers that attach before the first value share one execution. Anyone who subscribes after a value has been sent misses it, and that is the trap in the operator.
- If a late subscriber must see the most recent value, multicast through a `CurrentValueSubject` instead, or own that subject yourself and let callers subscribe to it.
- `makeConnectable()` with an explicit `connect()` removes the race outright: attach every subscriber first, then start the work.
- `share()` is reference counted, so when the last subscriber cancels the upstream is cancelled too, and the next subscriber triggers a completely fresh execution. It shares, it does not cache.
- This is one of the places Combine still genuinely beats async/await, where sharing a single in-flight operation means writing your own actor that holds the `Task` and hands out its value.

Inject the scheduler instead of hard-coding a queue, so the test can advance time by hand rather than waiting for it.

- Every time-based operator takes a `Scheduler`, so make it a dependency of the type: production passes the main queue, the test passes a controllable one.
- Combine ships `ImmediateScheduler`, which is enough for `receive(on:)` but not for `debounce` or `throttle`, since those need a virtual clock you can step forward. Teams either write a small test scheduler or use an existing one such as the scheduler package from Point-Free.
- `AnySchedulerOf<DispatchQueue>` keeps the property type identical in both configurations, which is what makes the injection painless.
- Without a virtual clock you are left with an expectation and a real wait, which makes the suite slow and flaky — and flaky performance-sensitive tests get muted, so the coverage is worse than none.
- Assert on behaviour rather than on operators: two fast keystrokes produce one request, a repeated query produces none, a new query cancels the one in flight.
- Collect output into an array from a `sink` and keep the cancellable alive for the whole test, otherwise the pipeline is torn down before anything is recorded.

Combine predates Sendable and has no isolation model, so almost every error is a closure carrying values across an isolation boundary the compiler will no longer take on trust.

- `sink` and the operator closures are checked for sendability now, so capturing a non-Sendable model or mutating main-actor state inside them is a compile error rather than a runtime gamble.
- `receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)` moves execution to the main thread but tells the type system nothing about actor isolation. The compiler still does not believe you are on the main actor, and that surprises people the most.
- The mechanical fixes, in order of preference: end the pipeline early and continue inside `Task { @MainActor in ... }`; make the values crossing the boundary `Sendable`, which often just means a struct instead of a class; or assert the isolation with `MainActor.assumeIsolated` where you can genuinely prove it.
- `assign(to: &$published)` remains the clean way to feed a `@Published` property on a main-actor model without writing a sink at all.
- `@preconcurrency import Combine` buys time on a large module, but treat it as a migration marker rather than a fix.
- Migrate module by module behind the upcoming-feature flags, and convert the simplest pipelines to async functions or `AsyncStream` as you go, since those carry isolation in the type system instead of fighting it.

Apple vends a short list: notifications, KVO, timers, URLSession tasks and your own `@Published` properties — everything else you write yourself.

- `NotificationCenter.default.publisher(for:)` covers system events, and the keyboard frame notifications are the classic UIKit use.
- `object.publisher(for: \.keyPath)` bridges KVO on Apple's own objects, such as a web view's estimated progress or a player item's status.
- `Timer.publish(every:on:in:)` is a connectable publisher, so it does nothing until `autoconnect()` or an explicit `connect()`.
- `URLSession.dataTaskPublisher(for:)` fits when the surrounding screen is already Combine; new code would call the async method instead.
- There is no built-in publisher for `UIControl`, which surprises people. Wrap target-action yourself, usually with a `UIAction` feeding a subject, or use the text-did-change notification for a text field.
- Binding back into UIKit is `assign(to:on:)`, which retains its target, so bind into a `@Published` property or use a `sink` with `[weak self]` when the target owns the pipeline.
- Store every cancellable in a `Set<AnyCancellable>` owned by the view controller and the whole graph is torn down with the screen.

Failure is part of a publisher's type, so `combineLatest` and `zip` refuse to compile until both sides agree on it, and any failure ends the subscription permanently.

- Align the error types first: `mapError` converts both sides to a shared type, `setFailureType(to:)` lifts a publisher whose failure is `Never`, and erasing both to the same `AnyPublisher` makes the boundary explicit.
- A completion is final. Once a publisher fails, the subscription is finished and nothing sent afterwards is delivered, which is exactly how a typeahead pipeline goes silently dead after one flaky request.
- `catch` swaps the failed publisher for a different one, so it can supply a cached value or a `Just`, but the original upstream is gone for good.
- `retry(n)` resubscribes to the upstream, so it helps only where resubscribing repeats the work — right for a network publisher, useless for a subject.
- The structural fix for a long-lived pipeline is to turn failure into a value: have the inner publisher emit a `Result` or your own state enum, and give the outer stream a `Never` failure type so it cannot die.
- `replaceError(with:)` is fine at the UI edge where a fallback is all you need, but log before you replace, or the bug becomes invisible.
